ai.definition: Reusable Lunar Landers are spacecraft designed to transport crew and cargo between a lunar orbiting gateway (such as Gateway) and the Moon's surface. These landers undergo multiple missions, reducing overall costs by reusing components.
ai.howItWorks: These landers use cryogenic or storable propellants, which are transferred from an orbiting gateway to the lander before descent. The engines are throttled during landing to ensure a soft touchdown on the lunar surface. After landing, the lander is refuelled and can be reused for subsequent missions.
ai.problemSolved: High costs associated with launching payloads and crew to the Moon multiple times. Reusability aims to reduce these costs by minimizing the number of launches required.
ai.manufacturing: Manufactured using advanced composite materials, lightweight structures, and high-efficiency engines to ensure durability and performance in lunar conditions.
ai.buildProcess: Components are fabricated separately and then integrated into a complete lander. Testing includes environmental simulations and rigorous ground tests before orbital operations.
ai.costDrivers: Development costs, material expenses, testing, and operational fuel requirements. High initial investment due to complex engineering and safety standards.
ai.lifecycleOutlook: Expected growth with increased lunar exploration efforts and potential establishment of a sustainable Moon presence.
ai.regulation: Regulated by international space laws, including those related to outer space activities and launch permits. Specific regulations may vary depending on the country or organization involved.
ai.risks: Technical risks such as engine reliability, material durability in harsh lunar conditions, and operational risks during refuelling and re-entry. Financial risks include high initial costs and uncertain market demand.
ai.profitability: Potential for profitability through reduced launch costs and increased efficiency in payload delivery. However, current economic models suggest it is still a nascent technology with limited revenue streams.
ai.futureDevelopment: Focus on improving engine performance, developing more durable materials, and enhancing automation to reduce human intervention during operations.

Rocket fuels that can be stored for extended periods without degradation, often used in satellite launches due to their longer shelf life.

subsystems.name: Descent stage
subsystems.role: brakes the vehicle out of lunar orbit and lands it softly on the surface.

subsystems.name: Ascent/crew module
subsystems.role: carries the crew up and down and is the only part that must survive the whole trip.

subsystems.name: Propellant system and depot
subsystems.role: stores cryogenic methane and oxygen for months and takes on more from a tanker in orbit.

subsystems.name: Avionics and landing sensors
subsystems.role: flies the descent without a pilot's eyes, avoiding boulders and craters.

subsystems.name: Power and thermal control
subsystems.role: keeps propellant liquid and electronics alive across the 14-day lunar night.

subsystems.name: Surface access and cargo handling
subsystems.role: gets crew and equipment from the cabin to the regolith.

subsystems.name: Docking and refuelling interface
subsystems.role: mates with an orbiting station or ferry craft and with tankers.

buildSteps.title: Design for reuse from the start
buildSteps.detail: Structures, tanks and engines are specified for multiple landing cycles, not one — which means fatigue-tolerant metals, inspectable welds and easily replaceable engine parts.

buildSteps.title: Build the pressure vessel and tanks
buildSteps.detail: Large stainless or aluminium-lithium tank domes are welded and pressure-tested; the crew cabin is a separate pressure vessel with a hatch and windows.

buildSteps.title: Install engines and plumbing
buildSteps.detail: Throttleable engines, feed lines, valves and cryogenic insulation go on, with redundancy so one engine failure is survivable during the final descent.

buildSteps.title: Fit avionics and landing sensors
buildSteps.detail: Computers, lidar, cameras and inertial units are installed and the landing software is trained on high-resolution lunar terrain data.

buildSteps.title: Test on the ground
buildSteps.detail: Propulsion, tanking, docking and life support are exercised in vacuum chambers and on test stands; tethered hover tests prove the throttle control.

buildSteps.title: Launch and refuel in orbit
buildSteps.detail: The lander reaches low Earth orbit, then a series of tanker flights fills its tanks so it has the velocity change needed to reach lunar orbit.

buildSteps.title: Fly to lunar orbit and dock
buildSteps.detail: The lander cruises to the Moon, enters orbit and docks with a station or crew vehicle to take on astronauts.

buildSteps.title: Land, operate and relaunch
buildSteps.detail: After descent and surface work, the ascent stage lifts off; if the design is truly reusable, the vehicle is refuelled and flown again rather than discarded.

buildSteps.title: Refurbish between missions
buildSteps.detail: Engines, seals, avionics and insulation are inspected and replaced where worn, using surface or orbital infrastructure rather than returning the whole vehicle to Earth.

prerequisites.why: methane and oxygen must be moved between vehicles in microgravity — only small-scale demonstrations have been attempted, never a full ship-to-ship fill.
refuelling a lunar lander takes many tanker flights, which only makes sense with cheap, rapidly reusable launchers.
robotic landers have hit the surface repeatedly, but crewed landings need far higher confidence than uncrewed ones.
propellant boils off over months unless actively cooled or well insulated.
the technology exists from Earth-orbit and Apollo experience, but not yet with months-long loitering and reuse.

pathway.milestone: crewed lunar landers in development under the Artemis programme, with uncrewed cargo landers already flying
pathway.unlocks: cargo delivery and landing-software testing on the real surface.

pathway.milestone: the first crewed Artemis landing, then cargo and crew flights to an orbiting lunar station
pathway.unlocks: regular access and the start of sustained surface activity.

pathway.milestone: demonstrated orbital refuelling and lander reuse between missions
pathway.unlocks: cost per landing falls far enough for long-term bases.

pathway.milestone: propellant produced from lunar ice rather than shipped from Earth
pathway.unlocks: a self-sustaining transport loop rather than a one-way supply line.
